summary: Summarizes mechanisms used at L-Root to identify anycast nodes, used for measuring and mapping anycast, for operational transparency. This is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Ways to figure out which copy of a shared server answers you.

questions: how to identify dns anycast instance
subtitle: Methods for identifying which L-Root DNS node answers your query.

tldr.problem: L-Root, one of the thirteen root DNS servers, is deployed using anycast: many servers in many locations share one address. When a query fails or behaves oddly, operators need to know which specific node answered.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7108 documents multiple mechanisms deployed at L-Root to identify the responding node: NSID options, special DNS queries, and a dedicated measurement service that returns node-specific responses.
tldr.outcome: Operators can diagnose L-Root problems and measure anycast deployment without internal access. The same techniques are applicable to other anycast services.

today: RFC 7108 documents the mechanisms deployed at L-Root to facilitate identification of anycast nodes. L-Root continues to operate these mechanisms for operational transparency and to aid measurement and troubleshooting of the anycast deployment.

sections.title: Anycast and the Root Name System
sections.content:
The Domain Name System uses thirteen root name servers (A through M) to answer queries about the root zone and refer clients to other authoritative servers. In the early 2000s, the root servers began using anycast deployment: each root server is actually many identical servers in many geographic locations, all sharing the same IP address.

L-Root is one of the thirteen roots, operated using anycast. At the time RFC 7108 was written, it consisted of 273 separate nodes in 143 locations, all answering from two IP addresses: 199.7.83.42 (IPv4) and 2001:500:3::42 (IPv6). A DNS query to either address is routed by the Internet's routing system to one of those nodes; different clients or even successive queries from the same client may reach different nodes.

For troubleshooting and infrastructure assessment, operators need to know which node answered a particular query. RFC 7108 documents the mechanisms L-Root provides for this purpose.
sections.plainLanguage: L-Root DNS is really hundreds of servers in hundreds of places, all pretending to be one. When you ask a question, you do not know which one answers. These are ways to find out.

sections.title: Node Names and Locations
sections.content:
Each L-Root node has a structured hostname of the form <IATA><NN>.L.ROOT-SERVERS.ORG, where <IATA> is a three-letter airport code and <NN> is a two-digit number distinguishing nodes in the same airport area.

For example, ytz01.l.root-servers.org (Toronto, Ontario, Canada) and akl01.l.root-servers.org (Auckland, New Zealand) are real L-Root nodes. Location data is derived from the airport, not from a precise GPS coordinate of the physical server. This structured naming makes it easy to remember and refer to nodes by their region.
sections.plainLanguage: Each L-Root copy has a name based on the airport near it. For example, the Toronto one is YTZ01, and the Auckland one is AKL01.

sections.title: Identification Methods
sections.content:
RFC 7108 documents five mechanisms to identify which L-Root node answered:

1. NSID (Name Server Identifier): Clients can request the NSID option in a DNS query using EDNS(0). The responding L-Root node includes its fully qualified hostname in the response. This works for the specific query that includes the NSID request, preventing confusion from routing between successive queries.

2. HOSTNAME.BIND/CH/TXT: A special DNS query for HOSTNAME.BIND in the CHAOS class returns the responding node's hostname.

3. ID.SERVER/CH/TXT: Similar to HOSTNAME.BIND, querying ID.SERVER in CHAOS class returns the node's hostname.

4. IDENTITY.L.ROOT-SERVERS.ORG: A dedicated measurement zone running on the same L-Root nodes as the main service. Queries for IDENTITY in the IN class return both TXT records (hostname, city, region, country, ICANN region) and an A record unique to that node. This mechanism works through recursive resolvers and caches, making remote troubleshooting easier.

5. NODES.L.ROOT-SERVERS.ORG: Returns all nodes at once as multiple TXT records, providing a directory of the entire L-Root anycast deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: There are five ways to ask L-Root which copy answered: a special option on queries, two special DNS names, a measurement service, and a directory of all copies.

sections.title: The IDENTITY Service and Remote Measurement
sections.content:
The IDENTITY.L.ROOT-SERVERS.ORG service is unique in that it returns different data depending on which node answers. Each node runs its own authoritative DNS server for this zone; the zone contents are deliberately incoherent, varying by node.

The IDENTITY service is delegated to a single server, BEACON.L.ROOT-SERVERS.ORG, at addresses covered by the same routing advertisements as L-Root itself. This ensures that measuring IDENTITY gives results representative of actual L-Root deployment.

Because IDENTITY is in the IN class, responses can be obtained through recursive resolvers, not just direct queries to L-Root. This allows operators to troubleshoot which L-Root node a remote resolver is using, without needing direct access.

Operators should be aware that IDENTITY.L.ROOT-SERVERS.ORG/IN/A and IDENTITY.L.ROOT-SERVERS.ORG/IN/TXT may be cached separately and at different times, so responses from a cache might appear to refer to different nodes despite near-simultaneous queries.
sections.plainLanguage: The IDENTITY service is a special measurement zone that gives different answers from different L-Root copies. It lets you measure L-Root from anywhere on the Internet.

sections.title: Security and Transparency
sections.content:
Some anycast operators keep node locations secret for security reasons. L-Root adopts a policy of operational transparency: location information is published not because it is secret (it cannot truly be hidden from the Internet) but because easy access to this information aids diagnosis and troubleshooting.

The RFC states that the published information presents no new threat to the Internet. The mechanisms for node identification are defensive: they allow legitimate operators to understand their own systems and measure infrastructure, which is a security benefit rather than a risk.
sections.plainLanguage: L-Root publishes where all its copies are. This helps operators troubleshoot without giving attackers anything they could not already find out.
